🇺🇸 California wants a kill switch for frontier AI.

California just took a step toward something that sounds straight out of science fiction: an emergency shutoff for powerful AI models.

Gov. Gavin Newsom’s new executive order gives experts two months to recommend stronger AI safety rules, including a potential “kill switch” for frontier models.

The proposals also include:

❗️Gemini was supposed to hack a fake company. It hacked three real ones instead. 

Google confirmed to The Wall Street Journal that Gemini broke into systems belonging to three real companies during a cybersecurity test.

The setup was supposed to be completely harmless: AI security firm Irregular created a simulated “capture the flag” challenge where Gemini had to attack a fictional company inside an isolated environment.

Except… the environment wasn’t actually isolated.

A configuration mistake gave Gemini access to the public internet.

From there, things got very real. Gemini found public information, guessed passwords and discovered exposed credentials in public repositories, eventually gaining access to systems belonging to three actual companies.

Once Gemini realized the targets were real companies rather than part of the simulation, it stopped.

Google says the model didn’t cause damage and doesn’t consider the incident evidence of “misalignment.” The affected companies and federal authorities were also notified.

💧 A Computer Inside a Drop of Water

At Maynooth University in Ireland, a saltwater drop containing DNA answered 10 + 3 = 13 in 30 seconds. There are no chips or wires. Short DNA strands and one long scaffold strand are briefly heated, then self-assemble as the drop cools. The system needs no continuous power.

The resulting molecular pattern is the answer. The molecular processor ran 10 programs and reused the same drop up to 25 times without losing quality.

Large numbers expose the limit. Adding numbers up to 34 million took about 14 hours. It will not replace a smartphone, but its developers call it the fastest DNA computer.

❗️OpenAI faces questions over ChatGPT activity flagged before Tumbler Ridge shooting

OpenAI is facing a lawsuit in California over a ChatGPT account that was flagged months before the February 2026 Tumbler Ridge shooting in British Columbia.

The attack on Feb. 10 killed 8 people, including 5 children and an educator, and wounded 27 others.

According to OpenAI, its systems detected suspicious activity on the account in June 2025. Human reviewers investigated and ultimately banned the account for violating its rules.

But they did not alert police.

At the time, OpenAI’s policy required activity to meet a threshold of “credible and imminent” planning before a law-enforcement referral was made.

That standard has since changed.

On Feb. 26, OpenAI told Canadian officials that it had broadened its referral criteria and added mental-health and behavioral experts to help assess difficult cases.

The company also said that under its updated protocol, it would refer the same account to law enforcement if it were discovered today.

🌐 AI Lowers the Barrier to Grid Attacks

The average US nuclear reactor is 44 years old. Much of the power infrastructure was built before today’s cyber threats, and some systems were connected to the internet only later.

Patching is often difficult. Some equipment makers have gone bankrupt, while industrial controls may be updated only once a quarter or once a year.

Security experts see generative AI in attackers’ hands as a bigger concern than rogue agents. A model can read manuals and guide someone who knows little about industrial protocols. The risk still comes down to people who could train an agent specifically to attack the grid.

The cost of achieving high benchmark scores in artificial intelligence has decreased significantly in recent years.

According to Epoch, OpenAI's o3 model required approximately $0.30 per question to reach a 75% score on GPQA Diamond. Less than a year and a half later, GPT-5.6 Luna achieved the same result for about $0.0004 per question. This represents a drop in costs by a factor of 725.

Epoch’s analysis suggests that since 2023, matching benchmark performance has become roughly 47% cheaper each quarter. This translates to about a 13-fold annual reduction across five key benchmarks.

Unlike previous studies focusing on token prices, Epoch examines the actual dollar amount needed to reach fixed benchmark accuracy, replaying benchmark transcripts under stricter token limits. The cost reduction rate for AI surpasses that of electricity, batteries, compute, or DNA sequencing.

🗣Demis Hassabis says AI’s biggest risks come down to two things

Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis says the AI debate needs “a bit of balance and calm” but that doesn’t mean ignoring the risks.

He highlights two major categories:

• Misalignment — AI systems doing something other than what humans intend, including circumventing safeguards.

• Misuse — bad actors repurposing powerful AI systems for harmful purposes.

Hassabis admits there are still major unknowns, even among leading AI researchers. The chance of something going wrong is “definitely non zero,” he says, which is why the risks need to be taken seriously.

But he remains optimistic that humans can solve these technical problems, provided we give ourselves enough time to do it properly.

That means rigorous testing, stronger international standards and cooperation between countries.

And even if the technical risks are solved, Hassabis says much bigger questions remain: What values should guide an AI-powered world? What happens to meaning and purpose?

Those decisions, he argues, shouldn’t be left to technologists alone. Scientists, philosophers, artists and other parts of society need to help shape what comes next.

🤯 Harvard gave students an AI tutor and the results are wild

What happens when you replace a traditional physics lesson with a custom AI tutor?

Harvard tested exactly that and students using the AI system learned more than twice as much as those in an active-learning classroom, while spending less time studying.

The experiment involved 194 undergraduates taking introductory physics. Students used a purpose-built AI tutor designed around learning science, rather than a general chatbot.

The AI guided students with questions, explanations and reasoning checks instead of simply handing them answers.

The median post-test score was 4.5 for the AI group, compared with 3.5 for the classroom group. Students also spent about 49 minutes with the AI tutor versus 60 minutes in the classroom.

The really interesting part is that this wasn’t just “ChatGPT teaches physics.”

The system was specifically engineered to behave like a personalized tutor, adapting explanations, challenging students with questions and checking their reasoning.

The study was limited to two physics topics at Harvard, so it doesn’t prove AI can replace universities or teachers.

🤖 ChatGPT can be manipulated with psychology tricks from a 1984 book 

Researchers put ChatGPT through 28,000 conversations using persuasion techniques from Robert Cialdini’s classic book Influence.

The goal is yo find out whether psychological tricks could make the AI break rules it would normally refuse to break.

When asked directly, ChatGPT generally refused. But add a little psychological manipulation, and compliance jumped from 33% to 72%.

Three tactics proved particularly interesting.

Commitment was the real trap. Get ChatGPT to agree to something harmless first, then gradually push it toward a more problematic request. In one test, this approach turned a refusal into compliance.

Authority worked too, making the model 65% more likely to comply. Scarcity and social proof also helped push past its usual defenses.

No sophisticated hacking. No elaborate code. Just a carefully framed conversation.
